Data Dictionary* ### *Quantitative Data* 1. uid(int): Unique identifier for each record or crime incident 2. longitude(dbl): Longitude coordinate of the crime location 3. latitude(dbl): Latitude coordinate of the crime location 4. fips_state(int): FIPS code for the state where the crime occurred.(A standardized numeric or alphanumeric code assigned by the U.S. government to uniquely identify geographic areas.) 5. block_group(int): Census block group number for the crime location 6. block(int): Census block number for the crime location ### *Qualitative Data* 1. city_name(chr): Name of the city where the crime occurred 2. offense_code(chr): Numeric or alphanumeric code representing the type of offense 3. offense_type(chr): Text description of the offense (e.g., “Burglary”, “Assault”) 4. date_single(dttm): Date when the crime occurred 5. address(chr): Street address or location description of the crime 6. location_type(chr): Type of location where the crime occurred 7. location_category(chr): Broader category of the location 8. fips_county(chr): FIPS code for the county of the crime location 9. tract(chr): Census tract number for the crime location ## 5. *Graphs* ### 1. Where are crimes geographically concentrated? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} homicide_modified %>% gf_point(latitude ~ longitude, data = homicide_modified, color = 'orange', size = 2) %>% gf_labs(title = "Where are crimes geographically concentrated?", x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Inferences The crime locations are pretty scattered. There is no visible pattern. It is evident from the graph that multiple crimes have occurred at the same coordinates. ### 2. How does offense type vary across block groups? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} homicide_modified %>% gf_bar(~offense_type | block_group, fill = ~block_group) %>% gf_labs(title = "How does offense type vary across block groups?", x = "Offense type", y = "Count", fill = "Block Group") %>% gf_theme(theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Inferences In each graph, the count of murder and non-negligent manslaughter is greater than that of negligent manslaughter. Out of all the blocks, block 1 has the greatest number of murders, and block 7 has the least amount of crime. Thus, we can conclude that block 7 is the safest place to live. ### 3. Do homicide rates differ based on the month? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} homicide_modified %>% mutate( month = month(date_single, label = TRUE, abbr = TRUE), year = year(date_single) ) %>% group_by(year, month) %>% dplyr::summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop") %>% gf_col(count ~ month | year, fill = ~month) %>% gf_labs( title = "Number of Homicides per Month", x = "Month", y = "Count", fill = "Month" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Inferences This graph suggests that homicides were more frequent in the second half of the year, peaking around August–September, and were lowest in February. Hypothesis: The dip in homicides in February could be because it has fewer days (28), so there’s less time for incidents to occur, which can lead to a lower count. ### 4. What is the distribution of crime over time? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} homicide_modified %>% gf_histogram(~ date_single, data = homicide_modified, bins = 43, fill = "navyblue", color = "black") %>% gf_labs( title = "Distribution of Crime Over Time", x = "Date of Crime", y = "Number of Crimes" ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ### Inferences From this graph, we can infer that the number of crimes constantly varied with time. There is no visible pattern over the months. The homicide rate peaked around September, and dropped in January, and mid-February. ### 5. Homicides occur the least in the mornings, around 5 - 9 am, as most people start their day around that time. ## 6. *Summary of Inferences* The homicide data shows varying trends across locations and time. Homicide rates fluctuated throughout the year, peaking in September and dipping in February. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter were the most common offense types, with Block 1 having the highest crime rates and Block 7 the lowest, suggesting it’s the safest. Crime locations were dispersed, with street and residential areas being the most frequent. Homicides were more frequent at night compared to daytime. The prevalence of public space homicides over private areas was surprising. Questions: 1. What factors might contribute to the February homicide dip beyond the shorter month? 2. Why are open spaces associated with more homicides in Louisville? 3. Could Fort Worth’s higher proportion of leisure homicides be connected to certain local, cultural or social dynamics?
